findings.title: Denial cache key does not include identity type
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, the raw subject identifier, action, name and parent. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and the render service (render:0) both have identifier "0", and user/service-account identifiers can also overlap. If an anonymous check for dashboards:read on dash1 is denied and cached, a subsequent render-service check for the same action/name/parent hits that denial at service.go:117 and returns Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions grants the renderer read access to all dashboards/folders. Different identity types must not share denial entries; include the identity type (or identity-specific prefixes like the permission cache uses) in the key.

findings.title: Every distinct cache-negative Check now issues a fresh permissions DB query
findings.body: When cached permissions do not allow the request, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions no longer consult permCache before querying permissionStore. The denial cache is per user+action+name+parent, so it only suppresses repeats for the exact same resource. Checking N different dashboards/folders a user cannot access (e.g. an authorizer evaluating many objects, or a client probing/enumerating UIDs) therefore causes N sequential SQL permission queries for the same user/action, even though the scope map was already fetched and refreshed by the first query; singleflight only coalesces concurrent identical calls. This defeats the 30s permission cache for denial-heavy workloads and amplifies DB load proportional to distinct resource names.

findings.title: Cached denial blocks access immediately after a grant or resource creation
findings.body: Any DB-confirmed denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s), and lines 116-121 return that denial without re-querying permissions. If the denied check happened just before the resource was created or before a permission/role was granted for that same name/parent (a common pre-creation or permission-assignment flow), the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s, which is exactly the newly-created dashboard/folder scenario this PR aims to fix. The denial timestamp also starts after the underlying permission/team/role caches were populated, so it can extend staleness beyond their expiry.

findings.title: List still serves stale cached permissions, so newly created resources do not appear
findings.body: List returns getCachedIdentityPermissions whenever the cache lookup succeeds, with no revalidation, freshness check, or DB fallback. If a user creates a dashboard/folder (adding a permission not present in the cached scope map) and then lists dashboards/folders within the 30s permCache TTL, the new resource is omitted from the List response even though a Check for that same resource would now re-query the DB and allow it. This leaves Check and List inconsistent and does not fully deliver the stated goal of letting users fetch newly created dashboards/folders.

findings.title: DB fallback does not refresh team, basic-role or folder-tree caches before caching a denial
findings.body: The fallback at lines 139-155 re-queries only the permission rows: getUserPermissions still obtains basic role and team memberships from basicRoleCache/teamCache, and the second checkPermission still obtains ancestors from the cached folderCache via buildFolderTree. If access should be granted because of a recent team/role change or via a newly created intermediate folder, the fallback still evaluates with the stale role/team/folder-tree data, returns false, and then writes a fresh 30s denial entry, extending the incorrect denial beyond the expiry of those underlying caches. Re-querying permissions alone is insufficient for inherited or role/team-based grants.

findings.title: Denial key uses raw subject identifier and ambiguous underscore concatenation
findings.body: permDenialKey is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the subject, whereas permCache is keyed by the canonical UID returned by GetUserIdentifiers. The same person addressed as user:<numeric-id> versus user:<uid> therefore gets separate denial entries and inconsistent fast-path behaviour. Additionally userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so pairs such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key and one resource's denial can incorrectly deny the other for that user.
